question: When do Annex III high-risk AI system obligations become applicable?
comment: Top-ranked chunk (digital_omnibus idx26) states the '2 December 2027' answer verbatim, yet the generated answer ignores it entirely and instead answers a different question (Art.6(4)/Art.49 'before placed on market' self-assessment/registration timing) using chunks 2-3. Non-responsive despite perfect top-1 retrieval -- a pure generation-stage failure, not a retrieval failure. Citations list all 4 retrieved docs regardless of use (known echo-citation pattern).

question: By what date must AI systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(1) and Annex I (i.e. safety components of products already covered by other EU product-safety legislation) comply with the AI Act's high-risk requirements?
comment: Doc-level hit (digital_omnibus retrieved) but the specific amendment sentence (Art.113 point (c)(ii), '2 August 2028') was never surfaced -- retrieved digital_omnibus chunks cover different amendments (Art.43(3) notified-body designation date '28 January 2028', and unrelated recitals). Model correctly refused to guess/fabricate the date and transparently flagged what it did find, rather than hallucinating -- good abstention behavior masking a real chunk-level recall gap. Citations echo all 3 retrieved docs though only one is truly load-bearing.

question: What was the original application date for the AI Act's high-risk system requirements (Chapter III), before the Digital Omnibus amendment?
comment: One of the 2 known single-hop retrieval misses: expected_source_doc (ai_act_2024_1689.html Art.113) was never retrieved, but the exact fact ('2 August 2026') is independently stated in the retrieved digital_omnibus recital text (quoting the original date it superseded), so the pipeline got the right answer despite the doc-level automated-check failure -- a genuine false negative in doc-path-based retrieval scoring. Answer omits the golden answer's nuance that Annex III had no separate original carve-out. Over-cites 3 unused guidance docs (article_10/11/6).

question: Does the Digital Omnibus change when Chapters I and II of the AI Act apply?
comment: digital_omnibus is retrieved (rank3) but the chunk covers Articles 25/27/28, not the actual Art.113 amendment text (point 40(a)) that would confirm/deny a change -- that specific chunk (seen elsewhere in this set, e.g. Q2's rank3) was not retrieved here. The model's 'no change' conclusion for Chapters I/II is correct on the headline but is asserted without ever seeing the amendment text (only the old, pre-amendment Art.113 via the Service-Desk page, which explicitly warns it 'has not yet been updated'), and it drops the material carve-out (Art.5(1)(ba)/(bb) applying later, Dec 2026) that the golden answer treats as essential. Weak grounding for a confident answer.

question: Under Article 53 of the AI Act, are providers of open-source general-purpose AI models exempt from all obligations in Article 53(1)?
comment: Second known single-hop 'retrieval miss': expected_source_doc is the Service-Desk Article-53 page, but the identical legal text is retrieved from the primary regulation (ai_act_2024_1689.html, rank1) and independently confirmed by the Commission's GPAI scope guidelines (rank2/4) -- another doc-level false negative, this time with excellent chunk-level and citation quality. Answer is accurate but omits explicitly restating that the exemption doesn't apply to systemic-risk models (present in Art.53(2) itself and stated by the guidelines).

question: If a company builds an AI-powered CV-screening tool that processes candidates' employment history and health-related disability accommodation notes to shortlist applicants, would this system trigger GDPR obligations in addition to the AI Act?
comment: GDPR was never retrieved at all for this GDPR-cross-reference question -- every retrieved chunk is AI-Act-only. The answer correctly says 'Yes' and correctly quotes AI Act recital 10 ('does not affect existing Union data-protection law'), but never engages with the substantive analysis the question needs: that health/disability data is special-category data under GDPR Art.9, prohibited absent an Art.9(2) exception, or that this is also an Annex III high-risk employment use case. A shallow, generic 'GDPR still applies' answer standing in for real cross-reference analysis.

question: Does GDPR give a data subject any rights specifically about being subject to a fully automated hiring or credit-scoring decision made by an AI system?
comment: Full Article 22 GDPR text retrieved at rank2 including paragraph 3's safeguards. Answer correctly states the right (Art.22(1)) and its three exceptions but omits paragraph 3 -- the human-intervention/express-view/contest-decision safeguards the golden answer treats as essential when an exception applies. Notably, this GDPR cross-reference succeeded where Q5 and Q8 (same doc, same difficulty tier) failed to retrieve GDPR at all -- an inconsistency in the retriever's handling of the adjacent-GDPR corpus worth investigating.

question: Does deploying a high-risk AI system that does systematic, large-scale profiling of individuals require a GDPR Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA), separately from any AI Act obligations?
comment: Clean result: Article 35(1)/(3)(a) GDPR retrieved at rank1 with the exact language needed, answer is accurate, complete, and correctly frames the DPIA as an independent, additional GDPR obligation. Best-performing GDPR cross-reference question in the set -- a useful positive control showing the pipeline can do this well when the right chunk is ranked first.

question: If an AI system used in recruitment processed special categories of personal data (e.g. data revealing racial or ethnic origin) to detect and correct algorithmic bias, is this permitted under GDPR on its own, or does something else need to apply?
comment: GDPR Art.9 itself was never retrieved (only indirect cross-references to 'Article 9(2), point (g)' inside AI Act/Digital-Omnibus recitals). The AI Act side of the answer (Art.10(5), the new Art.4a safeguard conditions a-f, and its extension via the Digital Omnibus to other providers/deployers) is excellent and fully grounded. But the GDPR-side framing ('GDPR alone does not permit this... conditions like explicit consent, employment necessity') is stated with a specificity not actually present in any retrieved chunk -- plausible background knowledge presented as if grounded, a faithfulness concern even though it happens to be correct. No GDPR citation given despite these specific GDPR claims.

question: Article 5(1)(h) of the AI Act prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement except in narrow cases. How does this provision interact with GDPR's rules on biometric data processing?
comment: The key 'without prejudice to Article 9 GDPR for purposes other than law enforcement' clause is retrieved (rank2, exact match). The answer's first section correctly restates this. However the 'Bottom line' section then asserts that GDPR rules 'still apply to the processing of biometric data for law-enforcement purposes (e.g., Article 9(1) of the GDPR, which allows processing for law enforcement...)' -- this contradicts the retrieved clause's own scoping ('for purposes OTHER than law enforcement') and is not how GDPR/LED actually divide jurisdiction (law-enforcement biometric processing is normally governed by the Law Enforcement Directive 2016/680, not GDPR Art.9). An inserted, unsupported claim that muddies an otherwise-correct core answer.

question: The AI Act Service Desk's summary of Article 113 says the Regulation 'shall apply from 2 August 2026', with earlier dates for certain chapters. Does the AI Act's own primary regulatory text (not just the Service Desk summary) confirm this same set of staggered dates?
comment: Excellent retrieval and a verbatim-accurate, fully grounded answer confirming the Service-Desk summary matches the primary EUR-Lex text. Worth flagging for self-consistency: this answer restates the pre-Digital-Omnibus Article 113 dates as simple fact with no caveat, whereas Q0-Q2 in this same set establish that those exact dates have since been superseded by the Digital Omnibus for Annex III/Annex I high-risk systems. Taken in isolation the answer is correct (the question narrowly asks about textual consistency between two mirrored, pre-amendment documents), but a user reading only this answer could walk away with an outdated understanding of the currently-applicable dates. digital_omnibus is cited but not actually used in the answer.

question: Article 53(1)(d) of the AI Act requires GPAI providers to publish a training-data-content summary 'according to a template provided by the AI Office.' Does the GPAI Code of Practice's Transparency Chapter clarify how this training-content-summary obligation relates to the more detailed Model Documentation Signatories must keep?
comment: Correct core relationship (Model Documentation vs. public training-content summary are related-but-distinct) grounded in the Transparency Chapter (rank1, exact match to golden answer). However the model's framing borrows the word 'complementary' and part of its reasoning from a different document -- the Copyright Chapter's boilerplate about Art.53(1)(c) vs (d) (rank5) -- rather than sourcing that language from the Transparency Chapter the question specifically asks about. A subtle cross-document conflation; the conclusion holds but the attribution blurs which Code chapter actually says what.

question: The AI Act Service Desk's Article 53 page mentions that open-source GPAI providers are exempt from Article 53(1)(a) and (b) unless the model has systemic risk. Where in the primary AI Act regulation text is this exception actually written, and does it match the Service Desk's summary?
comment: The single most serious error in this hard subset. The correct provision (Article 53(2), with its exact 'shall not apply to providers... unless the general-purpose AI models present systemic risks' text) IS present in the retrieved set (rank4, service_desk/article_53.html) but ranked below a near-identical-sounding but substantively different provision: Article 54(6), the authorised-representative open-source exemption (rank3, ai_act_2024_1689.html). The model confidently quotes Article 54(6) verbatim and states 'The exception is written directly in the AI Act itself, in Article 54, paragraph 6,' then claims this matches the Service Desk's description of the Article 53(1)(a)/(b) documentation exemption -- which it does not; Article 54(6) exempts a different obligation (the Article 54 authorised-representative duty) entirely. The quoted text is real and verbatim (not fabricated), but the legal-citation claim built around it is wrong. Directly contradicted by Q13 in this same set, where the identical underlying distinction (Art.53(2) vs. 54(6)) is drawn correctly -- a clear self-inconsistency, and the most consequential finding for a compliance-facing tool, since it hands the user a confidently wrong statutory citation.

question: The Commission's GPAI scope guidelines describe an open-source exemption from Article 53(1)(a)-(b). Which article of the AI Act's own text, as also captured in the Service Desk's Article 53 page, establishes this exemption, and what condition removes it?
comment: Gets right what Q12 gets wrong: correctly identifies Article 53(2) as the source of the Art.53(1)(a)/(b) open-source exemption and correctly distinguishes Article 54(6) as the separate authorised-representative exemption -- exactly the distinction Q12 collapses. See Q12's comment for the direct self-inconsistency. Weaker on the second half of the question: it doesn't explicitly confirm the Service-Desk Article-53 page's framing, likely because the retrieved Service-Desk chunks (rank3 is pure site-navigation boilerplate; rank5 covers paragraphs 4-7, not paragraph 2) never surfaced the actual Art.53(2) text on that side -- a wasted retrieval slot on navigation noise. Citation list also includes an entirely irrelevant transparency_guidelines_article50.pdf.

question: A provider wants to know whether their chatbot needs both an Article 50(1) 'you are talking to an AI' disclosure and a GDPR Article 13/14 information notice. Do these two obligations serve the same purpose, or are they distinct requirements that could both apply to the same system?
comment: GDPR was never retrieved for this question either (a fourth such case in the set, alongside Q1/Q5/Q8) -- all 5 chunks come from the Article 50 transparency guidelines. The AI-Act side of the answer is well grounded (Art.50(1) purpose, and the 'additive to data-protection information duties' framing from section 5.3, rank2). But the GDPR Art.13/14 description ('purpose, legal basis, rights, etc.') is generic background knowledge, not sourced from any retrieved chunk, and -- most importantly -- the answer never surfaces the specific Art.13(2)(f)/14(2)(g) automated-decision-making/profiling disclosure requirement that is the actual reason these two notice regimes can require different content for an AI chatbot. A correct top-level 'yes, both apply' without the substantive cross-reference analysis the question is really testing for.
